--- title: "Plotly Chart" execute: warning: false error: false format: html: toc: true toc-location: right code-fold: show code-tools: true number-sections: true code-block-bg: true code-block-border-left: "#31BAE9" --- ![](images/Plotly-logo.png){width="650"} # Introduction to Plotly Plotly's Python graphing library makes it easy to create interactive, publication-quality graphs. This document demonstrates how to create various plots, including line plots, scatter plots, bar charts, box plots, histograms, and more. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(reticulate) py_require(c('plotly','pandas','seaborn','psutil','requests')) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import plotly print(plotly.__version__) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 6.2.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import seaborn as sns import plotly.express as px import pandas as pd # Load an example dataset tips = sns.load_dataset("tips") tips.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` total_bill tip sex smoker day time size 0 16.99 1.01 Female No Sun Dinner 2 1 10.34 1.66 Male No Sun Dinner 3 2 21.01 3.50 Male No Sun Dinner 3 3 23.68 3.31 Male No Sun Dinner 2 4 24.59 3.61 Female No Sun Dinner 4 ``` ::: ::: # Scatter Plot A scatter plot is used to visualize the relationship between two continuous variables. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="tip", y="total_bill") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Color by Group You can color the points based on a categorical variable to see how the relationship varies across different groups. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="tip", y="total_bill", color="sex") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Size by Group The size of the points can be mapped to a variable to add another dimension to the plot. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="tip", y="total_bill", size="size") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Line Plot A line plot is suitable for showing the trend of a variable over time. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} dowjones = sns.load_dataset("dowjones") dowjones.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Date Price 0 1914-12-01 55.00 1 1915-01-01 56.55 2 1915-02-01 56.00 3 1915-03-01 58.30 4 1915-04-01 66.45 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import plotly.express as px fig = px.line(dowjones, x="Date", y="Price") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Line Plot with Dots You can also add markers to the line plot to highlight the data points. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import plotly.express as px fig = px.line(dowjones, x="Date", y="Price", markers=True) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Color by Group You can plot multiple lines on the same plot to compare different groups. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import random # Create datasets for comparison dowjones2 = dowjones.copy() dowjones2['type'] = 'old' dowjones3 = dowjones.copy() dowjones3['Price'] = dowjones3['Price'] + random.random() * 200 dowjones3['type'] = 'new' dowjones4 = pd.concat([dowjones2, dowjones3], ignore_index=True) dowjones4 = dowjones4.sort_values('Date').reset_index(drop=True) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} dowjones4.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Date Price type 0 1914-12-01 55.000000 old 1 1914-12-01 202.637115 new 2 1915-01-01 204.187115 new 3 1915-01-01 56.550000 old 4 1915-02-01 56.000000 old ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import plotly.express as px fig = px.line(dowjones4, x="Date", y="Price", color='type') fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Histogram A histogram visualizes the distribution of a single continuous variable. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.histogram(tips, x="total_bill") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Color by Group You can create separate histograms for different groups to compare their distributions. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.histogram(tips, x="total_bill", color='sex', barmode='group') fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Bar Chart A bar chart is used to display categorical data with bars of lengths proportional to the values they represent. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.bar(tips, x='sex', y='total_bill', color='sex') fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Box Plot A box plot shows the distribution of a dataset, including the median, quartiles, and potential outliers. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.box(tips, y="total_bill") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Color by Group You can group box plots by a categorical variable to compare distributions. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.box(tips, y="total_bill", x='sex', color='sex') fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Strip Plot A strip plot is a scatter plot for a categorical variable, showing the distribution of data points. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.strip(tips, x="day", y="total_bill") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Color by Group You can color the points in a strip plot to distinguish between different groups. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.strip(tips, x="day", y="total_bill", color='sex') fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Facet Plot Facet plots create subplots for different subsets of the data, allowing for easy comparison. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", color="sex", facet_col="day") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Three Plots per Row You can control the layout of the facet grid by specifying the number of columns to wrap. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", color="sex", facet_col="day", facet_col_wrap=3) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Customizing Title, Size, and Axis Names ## Add Title You can add a title to your plot and center it. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="tip", y="total_bill", title="Total Bill Title").update_layout(title_x=0.5) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Adjust Size The size of the plot can be customized to fit your needs. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="tip", y="total_bill") fig.update_layout( autosize=False, width=200, height=200 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ```{.python .cell-code} fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Change Axis Names You can change the labels of the x and y axes for clarity. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="tip", y="total_bill", labels={ "tip": "New X Label", "total_bill": "New Y Label" }) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Applying Themes Plotly offers several built-in themes to change the appearance of your plots. ::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills} ## ggplot2 Theme This theme mimics the style of the popular `ggplot2` library in R. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="tip", y="total_bill", template="ggplot2") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Seaborn Theme This theme applies a style similar to the Seaborn library. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="tip", y="total_bill", template="seaborn") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Plotly Dark Theme This theme uses a dark background for a modern look. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} fig = px.scatter(tips, x="tip", y="total_bill", template="plotly_dark") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: # Saving a Plot To save a plot, you may need to install the `kaleido` package: `pip install -U kaleido`. ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} df = px.data.gapminder().query("continent=='Oceania'") fig = px.line(df, x="year", y="lifeExp", title='Life expectancy in Canada') ``` ::: # Animated Plot Plotly supports animations for many chart types, though smooth transitions are best supported for scatter and bar plots. More information can be found [here](https://plotly.com/python/animations/). ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import plotly.express as px df = px.data.gapminder() px.scatter(df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", animation_frame="year", animation_group="country", size="pop", color="continent", hover_name="country", log_x=True, size_max=55, range_x=[100, 100000], range_y=[25, 90]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Reference - [Plotly Python Library](https://plotly.com/python/)
